claim: Millions of distinct virus species likely exist.
source: Although millions of distinct virus species likely exist, only approximately 9000 are catalogued in GenBank's RefSeq database.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the total number of virus species that may exist in nature.

claim: Approximately 9000 virus species are catalogued in GenBank's RefSeq database.
source: Although millions of distinct virus species likely exist, only approximately 9000 are catalogued in GenBank's RefSeq database.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the number of catalogued viruses in a specific database.

claim: Over 2500 complete circular DNA virus genomes were annotated in a GenBank-compliant format using the Cenote-Taker pipeline.
source: A bioinformatics pipeline, Cenote-Taker, was developed to automatically annotate over 2500 complete genomes in a GenBank-compliant format.
evidence: The manuscript describes the development and application of a bioinformatics tool that annotated genomes from the study.

claim: The new genomes belong to dozens of established and emerging viral families.
source: The new genomes belong to dozens of established and emerging viral families.
evidence: This is supported by the taxonomic classification of genomes reported in the study.

claim: Some circular DNA viruses appear to be the result of previously undescribed recombination events between ssDNA and ssRNA viruses.
source: Some appear to be the result of previously undescribed recombination events between ssDNA and ssRNA viruses.
evidence: The manuscript presents genomic evidence of hybrid viruses with genes from both ssDNA and ssRNA viruses.

claim: Hundreds of circular DNA elements do not encode any discernable similarities to previously characterized sequences.
source: In addition, hundreds of circular DNA elements that do not encode any discernable similarities to previously characterized sequences were identified.
evidence: The manuscript describes 'dark matter' sequences with no recognizable homology to known sequences.

claim: An artificial neural network was used to identify candidate viral capsid proteins.
source: To characterize these 'dark matter' sequences, we used an artificial neural network to identify candidate viral capsid proteins, several of which formed virus-like particles when expressed in culture.
evidence: The manuscript describes the use of iVireons, an artificial neural network, to predict capsid proteins.

claim: Several predicted capsid proteins formed virus-like particles when expressed in culture.
source: To characterize these 'dark matter' sequences, we used an artificial neural network to identify candidate viral capsid proteins, several of which formed virus-like particles when expressed in culture.
evidence: The manuscript presents electron microscopy data showing particle formation from expressed proteins.

claim: A substantial fraction of reads and de novo assembled contigs in metagenomics efforts are binned as genetic 'dark matter' with no recognizable similarity to characterized sequences.
source: Although the bacterial populations in these surveys have become increasingly recognizable (Lloyd-Price et al., 2017), a substantial fraction of the reads and de novo assembled contigs in many metagenomics efforts are binned as genetic 'dark matter,' with no recognizable similarity to characterized sequences (Krishnamurthy and Wang, 2017; Oh et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on metagenomics.

claim: Some genetic dark matter consists of viral sequences that have remained poorly characterized due to their enormous diversity.
source: Some of this dark matter undoubtedly consists of viral sequences, which have remained poorly characterized due to their enormous diversity (Simmonds et al., 2017; Paez-Espino et al., 2016; Emerson et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on viral diversity.

claim: Understanding of viral diversity, even of viruses known to directly infect humans, has been incomplete.
source: Recent efforts have shown that our understanding of viral diversity, even of viruses known to directly infect humans, has been incomplete (Pastrana et al., 2018; Turnbaugh et al., 2007; Gilbert et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: All known cellular organisms encode conserved sequences such as ribosomal RNA genes that can readily be identified through sequence analysis.
source: Whereas all known cellular organisms encode conserved sequences (such as ribosomal RNA genes) that can readily be identified through sequence analysis, viruses, as a whole, do not have any universally conserved sequence components (O'Leary et al., 2016; Brister et al., 2015; Sullivan, 2015; Rohwer and Edwards, 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge in microbiology supported by citations.

claim: Viruses, as a whole, do not have any universally conserved sequence components.
source: Whereas all known cellular organisms encode conserved sequences (such as ribosomal RNA genes) that can readily be identified through sequence analysis, viruses, as a whole, do not have any universally conserved sequence components (O'Leary et al., 2016; Brister et al., 2015; Sullivan, 2015; Rohwer and Edwards, 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge in virology supported by citations.

claim: Success has been achieved in RNA virus discovery by probing for conserved sequences of RNA-dependent RNA polymerase or reverse transcriptase genes in metatranscriptomic data.
source: Nevertheless, some success has been achieved in RNA virus discovery by probing for the conserved sequences of their distinctive RNA-dependent RNA polymerase or reverse transcriptase genes in metatranscriptomic data (Shi et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Many bacteriophages of the order Caudovirales have been reported in high numbers due to their culturability and detectability using viral plaque assays.
source: Also, many bacteriophages of the order Caudovirales, such as the families Siphoviridae, Podoviridae, and Myoviridae, have been reported in high numbers due to their and their hosts' culturability and their detectability using viral plaque assays (Pope et al., 2015; Grose and Casjens, 2014; Grose et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Many small DNA viruses are not easily cultured.
source: In contrast, many small DNA viruses are not easily cultured (Bedell et al., 1991), use diverse genome replication strategies, and typically lack DNA polymerase genes such as those in large DNA viruses (Koonin et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Small DNA viruses use diverse genome replication strategies and typically lack DNA polymerase genes.
source: In contrast, many small DNA viruses are not easily cultured (Bedell et al., 1991), use diverse genome replication strategies, and typically lack DNA polymerase genes such as those in large DNA viruses (Koonin et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Many DNA virus genomes have circular topology, which allows selective enrichment through rolling circle amplification methods.
source: In contrast to the nuclear genomes of animals, many DNA virus genomes have circular topology, which allows selective enrichment through rolling circle amplification (RCA) methods (Kim et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge in virology supported by a citation.

claim: Viral capsids can protect nucleic acids from nuclease digestion and mediate migration of the viral genome through ultracentrifugation gradients or size exclusion columns.
source: Further, the unique ability of viral capsids to protect nucleic acids from nuclease digestion and to mediate the migration of the viral genome through ultracentrifugation gradients or size exclusion columns allows physical isolation of viral genomes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about viral capsid properties.

claim: 1844 novel circular sequences encode genes with similarity to proteins of ssDNA viruses.
source: Of the novel circular sequences detected in the survey, 1844 encode genes with similarity to proteins of ssDNA viruses and 55 encode genes with similarity to dsDNA viral proteins (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a direct result from the study's data analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: 55 novel circular sequences encode genes with similarity to dsDNA viral proteins.
source: Of the novel circular sequences detected in the survey, 1844 encode genes with similarity to proteins of ssDNA viruses and 55 encode genes with similarity to dsDNA viral proteins (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a direct result from the study's data analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The large majority of genomes from this study are highly divergent from RefSeq entries.
source: The large majority of genomes from this study are highly divergent from RefSeq entries (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by BLASTX analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: 868 genomes had similarity to unclassified eukaryotic viruses known as CRESS viruses.
source: We discovered 868 genomes that had similarity to unclassified eukaryotic viruses known as circular replication-associated protein (Rep)-encoding single-stranded DNA (CRESS) viruses.
evidence: This is a direct result from the study's taxonomic classification.

claim: CRESS viruses are defined by the presence of a characteristic rolling circle endonuclease/superfamily three helicase gene (Rep).
source: The group is defined by the presence of a characteristic rolling circle endonuclease/superfamily three helicase gene (Rep) (Zhao et al., 2019; Kazlauskas et al., 2019), but has not been assigned to families by the ICTV or RefSeq.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CRESS viruses supported by citations.

claim: 199 non-redundant unclassified CRESS virus genomes had been previously deposited in GenBank.
source: We estimate that 199 non-redundant unclassified CRESS virus genomes had been previously deposited in GenBank, and 85 are curated in RefSeq (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is an estimate based on database searches conducted by the authors.

claim: 670 complete Microviridae genomes were discovered.
source: Also abundant was the viral family Microviridae, a class of small bacteriophages, with 670 complete genomes.
evidence: This is a direct result from the study's genome discovery.

claim: This study represents a substantial expansion beyond the 459 non-redundant microvirus genomes previously listed in GenBank.
source: This represents a substantial expansion beyond the 459 non-redundant microvirus genomes previously listed in GenBank (of which 44 were curated in the RefSeq database).
evidence: This is a comparison of the study's results to existing database entries.

claim: Viral families were found in association with 23 different animal species.
source: Viral families were found in association with 23 different animal species (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is shown in the heatmap in Figure 1C.

claim: All animals are presumed to have microbial communities.
source: It was not surprising to find bacterial viruses, as all animals are presumed to have microbial communities and our sampling included tissues where these communities reside.
evidence: This is established knowledge in microbiology.

claim: 609 circular contigs appeared to represent elements that lacked discernable similarity to known viruses.
source: In addition to circular genomes with recognizable similarity to known viruses, 609 circular contigs appeared to represent elements that lacked discernable similarity to known viruses (Figure 1A,C).
evidence: This is a direct result from the study's sequence analysis.

claim: The vast majority of the de novo assembled circular genomes were <10 kb in length.
source: The vast majority of the de novo assembled circular genomes were <10 kb in length (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in the size distribution plot in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Large genomes are typically more difficult to de novo assemble from short reads.
source: This is largely due to the fact that large genomes are typically more difficult to de novo assemble from short reads.
evidence: This is established knowledge in bioinformatics.

claim: A new tailed bacteriophage with a 419 kb genome was detected.
source: Despite these technical obstacles, our detection of a new tailed bacteriophage with a 419 kb genome (Myoviridae sp. isolate ctbc_4, GenBank Accession: MH622943), along with 45 other >10 kb circular sequences (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), indicates that the methods used for the current work can detect large viral genomes.
evidence: This is a specific genome detected in the study with a GenBank accession number.

claim: 45 circular sequences greater than 10 kb were detected.
source: Despite these technical obstacles, our detection of a new tailed bacteriophage with a 419 kb genome (Myoviridae sp. isolate ctbc_4, GenBank Accession: MH622943), along with 45 other >10 kb circular sequences (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), indicates that the methods used for the current work can detect large viral genomes.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: There has been a recent renewal of interest in the hypothesis that viruses may be etiologically associated with degenerative brain diseases, such as Alzheimer's disease.
source: There has been a recent renewal of interest in the hypothesis that viruses may be etiologically associated with degenerative brain diseases, such as Alzheimer's disease (Itzhaki et al., 2016; Eimer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: Conflicting literature suggests the possible presence of papillomaviruses in human brain tissue.
source: Conflicting literature suggests the possible presence of papillomaviruses in human brain tissue (Coras et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Complete or partial genomes of known papillomaviruses, Merkel cell polyomavirus, and/or anelloviruses were observed in some brain samples.
source: Although complete or partial genomes of known papillomaviruses, Merkel cell polyomavirus, and/or anelloviruses were observed in some samples (Supplementary file 3), no novel complete viral genomes were recovered (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a result from the brain tissue analysis in the study.

claim: No novel complete viral genomes were recovered from brain samples.
source: Although complete or partial genomes of known papillomaviruses, Merkel cell polyomavirus, and/or anelloviruses were observed in some samples (Supplementary file 3), no novel complete viral genomes were recovered (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a negative result from the brain tissue analysis.

claim: No viral sequences were detected in a follow-up RNA deep sequencing analysis of the brain samples.
source: No viral sequences were detected in a follow-up RNA deep sequencing analysis of the brain samples.
evidence: This is a negative result from RNA sequencing.

claim: Certain nucleic acid extraction reagents are contaminated with viral nucleic acids.
source: It has recently become apparent that certain nucleic acid extraction reagents are contaminated with viral nucleic acids (Asplund et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: No evidence of sequences of viruses reported in this study were found in reagent-only control samples.
source: To ensure we were not merely reporting the sequences of the 'reagent virome,' we performed our wet bench and bioinformatic pipeline on three independent replicates of reagent-only samples. We found no evidence of sequences of any viruses reported here or elsewhere.
evidence: This is a result from control experiments conducted in the study.

claim: Almost no sequences were found in different animal samples, aside from technical replicates.
source: Further, cross-sample comparison of contigs showed that almost no sequences were found in different animal samples, aside from technical replicates.
evidence: This is a result from cross-sample comparison analysis.

claim: Six viral genomes were observed in multiple unrelated samples from at least two sequencing runs.
source: In total, six viral genomes were observed in multiple unrelated samples from at least two sequencing runs (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is a result from cross-sample comparison analysis.

claim: Six viral genomes found in multiple samples represent 0.24% of the genomes reported in the study.
source: It is unclear whether this small minority of genomes (0.24% of the genomes reported in the current study) represent reagent contamination, lab contamination, or actual presence of the sequences in different types of samples.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the study's data.

claim: In most samples, most reads did not align to the genomes reported in this study or virus genomes from RefSeq.
source: Given the stringent requirements for sequences to be considered as belonging to a complete viral genome, as well as the largely unexplored nucleotide space of the virome, it is unsurprising that, in most samples, most reads did not align to the genomes reported in this study or virus genomes from RefSeq (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is shown in the read mapping analysis in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Single stranded DNA viruses have vital genes encoding proteins that mediate genome replication, provide virion structure, and facilitate packaging of viral nucleic acid into the virion.
source: Single stranded DNA viruses, in general, have vital genes encoding proteins that mediate genome replication, provide virion structure, and, in some cases, facilitate packaging of viral nucleic acid into the virion.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ssDNA virus biology.

claim: Structurally conserved viral proteins tend to be important for evolutionary comparisons and can serve as 'hallmark genes' for virus discovery and characterization.
source: Being structurally conserved, these genes also tend to be important for evolutionary comparisons and can serve as important 'hallmark genes' for virus discovery and characterization.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the properties of conserved genes.

claim: Structurally conserved proteins sometimes do not have enough sequence conservation to be amenable to high confidence BLASTP searches.
source: However, even structurally conserved proteins sometimes do not have enough sequence conservation as to be amenable to high confidence BLASTP searches.
evidence: This is established knowledge in bioinformatics.

claim: Structures of hallmark genes of exemplar isolates from most established ssDNA virus families have been solved and deposited in publicly available databases such as PDB.
source: Structures of hallmark genes of exemplar isolates from most established ssDNA virus families have been solved and deposited in publicly available databases such as PDB (Protein Data Bank) (Burley et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the PDB database.

claim: HHpred can assign structural matches for a given gene based on the predicted potential folds of a given amino acid sequence.
source: Using bioinformatic tools, such as HHpred, one can assign structural matches for a given gene based on the predicted potential folds of a given amino acid sequence.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the HHpred tool.

claim: HHpred has been extensively tested and validated for computational structural modeling by the structural biology community.
source: HHpred has been extensively tested and validated for computational structural modeling by the structural biology community (Meier and Söding, 2015; Huang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Sequence similarity networks represent relationships between viral sequences better than phylogenetic trees.
source: Sequence similarity network analyses, it has been proposed (Iranzo et al., 2017), represent relationships between viral sequences better than phylogenetic trees.
evidence: This is a proposal from a previous study cited in the manuscript.

claim: SSNs have previously been used for viral protein and genome cluster comparison.
source: Further, SSNs have previously been used for viral protein and genome cluster comparison (Bolduc et al., 2017; Lima-Mendez et al., 2008; Lefeuvre et al., 2019; Kazlauskas et al., 2019) and can be used to display related groups of viral genes in two dimensions (Bin Jang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Sequences from this study expand and link smaller disconnected clusters of sequences found in GenBank entries.
source: The network shows that sequences from this study expand and link smaller disconnected clusters of sequences found in GenBank entries (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This is shown in the sequence similarity networks in Figure 2.

claim: A number of previously unknown clusters of capsid sequences were identified.
source: Perhaps more importantly a number of previously unknown clusters were identified, providing insight into highly divergent hallmark sequences and making this capsid sequence space amenable to BLAST searches in GenBank (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The satellite tobacco necrosis virus (STNV) capsid protein structure is highly similar to the capsid proteins of geminiviruses and other ssDNA viruses.
source: Although the satellite tobacco necrosis virus (STNV) capsid protein encapsidates an RNA molecule, it has previously been noted that its structure is highly similar to the capsid proteins of geminiviruses and other ssDNA viruses (Koonin et al., 2015; Kraberger et al., 2015; Krupovic et al., 2009; Hipp et al., 2017; Bottcher et al., 2004; Zhang et al., 2001) and was included as a model for populating this network.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: Rep genes have been the primary sequences used for taxonomy of CRESS viruses.
source: Rep genes have been the primary sequences used for taxonomy of CRESS viruses (Zhao et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: A network with alignment cutoffs with E values of 1 × 10−60 could split the Rep gene data neatly into 'family-level' clusters.
source: In this case, it was determined that a network with alignment cutoffs with E values of 1 × 10−60 could split the data neatly into 'family-level' clusters (Fontenele et al., 2019; Kraberger et al., 2019), precisely mirroring ICTV taxonomy of CRESS viruses.
evidence: This is a methodological finding from the study's network analysis.

claim: The family-level clustering of Rep genes precisely mirrors ICTV taxonomy of CRESS viruses.
source: In this case, it was determined that a network with alignment cutoffs with E values of 1 × 10−60 could split the data neatly into 'family-level' clusters (Fontenele et al., 2019; Kraberger et al., 2019), precisely mirroring ICTV taxonomy of CRESS viruses.
evidence: This is a result from the study's network analysis compared to ICTV taxonomy.

claim: Many additional family-level clusters can be discerned from unclassified CRESS viruses.
source: Many additional family-level clusters can be discerned from unclassified CRESS viruses.
evidence: This is an inference from the network analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: CRESS viruses appear to be ubiquitous among eukaryotes.
source: Although no single family of viruses accounts for the majority of genomes in this study, these results expand the knowledge of the vast diversity of CRESS viruses, which appear to be ubiquitous among eukaryotes (Krupovic et al., 2016; Zerbini et al., 2017; Rosario et al., 2017; Varsani and Krupovic, 2018) and are likely to also infect archaea (Díez-Villaseñor and Rodriguez-Valera, 2019; Kazlauskas et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CRESS viruses are likely to also infect archaea.
source: Although no single family of viruses accounts for the majority of genomes in this study, these results expand the knowledge of the vast diversity of CRESS viruses, which appear to be ubiquitous among eukaryotes (Krupovic et al., 2016; Zerbini et al., 2017; Rosario et al., 2017; Varsani and Krupovic, 2018) and are likely to also infect archaea (Díez-Villaseñor and Rodriguez-Valera, 2019; Kazlauskas et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Characterized CRESS viruses have small icosahedral virions (20–30 nm in diameter) with a simple T = 1 geometry.
source: Characterized CRESS viruses have small icosahedral virions (20–30 nm in diameter) with a simple T = 1 geometry (Khayat et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge about CRESS virus structure supported by a citation.

claim: The T = 1 capsid architecture likely limits genome size, as nearly all previously reported CRESS virus genomes and genome segments are under 3.5 kb.
source: This capsid architecture likely limits genome size, as nearly all previously reported CRESS virus genomes and genome segments are under 3.5 kb.
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between capsid structure and genome size.

claim: Bacilladnaviruses have 4.5–6 kb genomes.
source: Exceptions to this size rule are bacilladnaviruses, which have 4.5–6 kb genomes (Tomaru et al., 2011) and cruciviruses, which have 3.5–5.5 kb genomes (Quaiser et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Cruciviruses have 3.5–5.5 kb genomes.
source: Exceptions to this size rule are bacilladnaviruses, which have 4.5–6 kb genomes (Tomaru et al., 2011) and cruciviruses, which have 3.5–5.5 kb genomes (Quaiser et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The genomes of larger CRESS viruses encode capsid genes that appear to have been acquired horizontally from RNA viruses.
source: Interestingly, the genomes of these larger CRESS viruses encode capsid genes that appear to have been acquired horizontally from RNA viruses (Kazlauskas et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Eight CRESS-like circular genomes in this dataset exceed 6 kb in length.
source: In our dataset, eight CRESS-like circular genomes exceed 6 kb in length (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Large CRESS genomes in this study are apparently attributable to several independent acquisitions of capsid genes from other taxa and/or capsid gene duplication events.
source: Further, this study's large CRESS genomes are apparently attributable to several independent acquisitions of capsid genes from other taxa and/or capsid gene duplication events.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genomic analysis of large CRESS viruses.

claim: CRESS virus isolate ctdh33 encoded three separate genes with structural homology to STNV capsid.
source: Notably, a large CRESS genome (CRESS virus isolate ctdh33, associated with rhabditid nematodes that were serially cultured from a soil sample) encoded three separate genes with structural homology (HHpred probability scores 97–99%) to STNV capsid (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is a result from HHpred structural prediction analysis.

claim: The three predicted STNV capsid homologs in CRESS virus ctdh33 are highly divergent from one another, with only 28–30% amino acid similarity.
source: The three predicted STNV capsid homologs in the nematode virus are highly divergent from one another, with only 28–30% amino acid similarity, but also highly divergent from other amino acid sequences in GenBank.
evidence: This is a result from sequence comparison analysis.

claim: The capsid gene array in CRESS virus ctdh33 is possibly the result of gene duplication events.
source: A possible explanation for this observation is that the capsid gene array is the result of gene duplication events.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed gene arrangement.

claim: CRESS genomes ctba10, ctcc19, ctbj26, ctcd34, and ctbd1037 each encode two divergent capsid gene homologs.
source: CRESS genomes ctba10, ctcc19, ctbj26, ctcd34, and ctbd1037 (ranging from 3.5 to 6.2 kb in length) also each encode two divergent capsid gene homologs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B,C,E,H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Single genomes encoding multiple capsid genes with related but distinct amino acid sequences have been observed in RNA viruses.
source: Single genomes encoding multiple capsid genes with related but distinct amino acid sequences have been observed in RNA viruses (Agranovsky et al., 1995) and giant dsDNA viruses (Schulz et al., 2017), but we believe that this is the first time it has been reported in ssDNA viruses.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Single genomes encoding multiple capsid genes with related but distinct amino acid sequences have been observed in giant dsDNA viruses.
source: Single genomes encoding multiple capsid genes with related but distinct amino acid sequences have been observed in RNA viruses (Agranovsky et al., 1995) and giant dsDNA viruses (Schulz et al., 2017), but we believe that this is the first time it has been reported in ssDNA viruses.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: This is the first time multiple capsid genes with related but distinct amino acid sequences have been reported in ssDNA viruses.
source: Single genomes encoding multiple capsid genes with related but distinct amino acid sequences have been observed in RNA viruses (Agranovsky et al., 1995) and giant dsDNA viruses (Schulz et al., 2017), but we believe that this is the first time it has been reported in ssDNA viruses.
evidence: This is a claim by the authors based on their literature review.

claim: Two related large CRESS viruses (ctdb796 and ctce741) encode capsid proteins similar to those of bacilladnaviruses.
source: Two related large CRESS viruses (ctdb796 and ctce741) encode capsid proteins similar to those of bacilladnaviruses (Figure 4—figure supplement 1K,M).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Rep genes of CRESS viruses ctdb796 and ctce741 do not show close similarity to known bacilladnavirus Reps.
source: Interestingly, the Rep genes of the two viruses do not show close similarity to known bacilladnavirus Reps and are instead similar to the Reps of certain unclassified CRESS viruses, suggesting that CRESS ctdb796 and CRESS ctce741 are representatives of a new hybrid CRESS virus family.
evidence: This is a result from sequence comparison analysis.

claim: CRESS viruses ctdb796 and ctce741 are representatives of a new hybrid CRESS virus family.
source: Interestingly, the Rep genes of the two viruses do not show close similarity to known bacilladnavirus Reps and are instead similar to the Reps of certain unclassified CRESS viruses, suggesting that CRESS ctdb796 and CRESS ctce741 are representatives of a new hybrid CRESS virus family.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genomic analysis of these viruses.

claim: CRESS virus genomes ctca5 and ctgh4 encode capsid genes that show amino acid similarity to distinct groups of icosahedral T = 3 ssRNA virus capsids.
source: Two other CRESS virus genomes (isolates ctca5 and ctgh4) encode capsid genes that show amino acid similarity to distinct groups of icosahedral T = 3 ssRNA virus capsids (Makino et al., 2013) (tombus- and tombus-like viruses), but not to cruciviruses or bacilladnaviruses (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D,J, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4 and related supplementary figures.

claim: A 6.6 kb CRESS virus (isolate ctbd466) was found to encode a gene with some similarity to the capsid region of the polyprotein of two newly described ssRNA viruses.
source: Further, a 6.6 kb CRESS virus (isolate ctbd466) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1L) was found to encode a gene with some similarity to the capsid region of the polyprotein of two newly described ssRNA viruses (ciliovirus and brinovirus (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B) (Makino et al., 2013; Greninger and DeRisi, 2015).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1L and 2B.

claim: Protein fold predictor Phyre2 showed a top hit (58% confidence) for the capsid protein of a norovirus for CRESS virus isolate ctbd466.
source: Protein fold predictor Phyre2 (Kelley et al., 2015) showed a top hit (58% confidence) for the capsid protein of a norovirus (ssRNA virus with T = 3 icosahedral capsid) for isolate ctbd466 (see GenBank: AXH73946).
evidence: This is a result from Phyre2 structural prediction analysis.

claim: Two CRESS genomes (ctbe30 and ctbc27) combine Rep genes specific to CRESS viruses with several genes specific to inoviruses.
source: Two CRESS genomes (ctbe30 and ctbc27) from separate Rhesus macaque stool samples combine Rep genes specific to CRESS viruses with several genes specific to inoviruses, including inovirus-like capsid genes, which encode proteins that form a filamentous virion (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F,N).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F,N.

claim: The bacteriophage families Inoviridae and Microviridae are ssDNA viruses that replicate via the rolling circle mechanism.
source: The bacteriophage families Inoviridae and Microviridae are ssDNA viruses that replicate via the rolling circle mechanism, but they are not considered conventional CRESS viruses because they exclusively infect prokaryotes and do not encode Rep genes with CRESS-like sequences.
evidence: This is established knowledge about these bacteriophage families.

claim: Inoviridae and Microviridae are not considered conventional CRESS viruses because they exclusively infect prokaryotes and do not encode Rep genes with CRESS-like sequences.
source: The bacteriophage families Inoviridae and Microviridae are ssDNA viruses that replicate via the rolling circle mechanism, but they are not considered conventional CRESS viruses because they exclusively infect prokaryotes and do not encode Rep genes with CRESS-like sequences.
evidence: This is established knowledge about viral taxonomy.

claim: CRESS genomes ctbe30 and ctbc27 encode homologs of zonular occludens toxin (ZOT) and RstB.
source: Other inovirus-like genes encoded in the ctbe30 and ctbc27 genomes include homologs of zonular occludens toxin (ZOT, a packaging ATPase) and RstB (a DNA-binding protein required for host genome integration) (Falero et al., 2009) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F,N).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F,N.

claim: TBLASTX searches using ctbe30 and ctbc27 sequences yielded large segments of similarity to various bacterial chromosomes.
source: TBLASTX searches using ctbe30 and ctbc27 sequences yielded large segments of similarity to various bacterial chromosomes (e.g., GenBank accession numbers AP012044 and AP018536), presumably representing integrated prophages.
evidence: This is a result from TBLASTX searches.

claim: CRESS viruses ctbe30 and ctbc27 represent a previously undescribed bacteria-tropic branch of the CRESS virus supergroup.
source: This suggests that ctbb30 and ctbc27 represent a previously undescribed bacteria-tropic branch of the CRESS virus supergroup.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genomic analysis and BLAST results.

claim: Viral genomes discussed in the large CRESS virus section were validated by aligning individual reads back to the contigs followed by visual inspection.
source: Viral genomes discussed in this section were validated by aligning individual reads back to the contigs followed by visual inspection.
evidence: This describes a validation method used in the study.

claim: No disjunctions were detected in read alignments, indicating that illegitimate recombinations are not evident.
source: No disjunctions were detected, indicating that illegitimate recombinations are not evident (see Figure 4—figure supplement 2C for an example).
evidence: This is a result from the validation analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Potential viral 'dark matter' was defined as circular contigs with no hits with E values < 1 × 10−5 in BLASTX searches of a database of viral and plasmid proteins.

claim: Groups of related dark matter elements (dark matter genome groups, DMGGs) can be delineated by the presence of a conserved, group-specific marker gene.
source: Further, groups of related dark matter elements (i.e. dark matter genome groups (DMGGs)), much like viral families, could be delineated by the presence of a conserved, group-specific marker gene.
evidence: This is a methodological approach developed in the study.

claim: DMPC7 and DMPC17 ORFs are always observed in genomes with a DMPC1 ORF (i.e., DMGG1).

claim: Sequences of capsid genes are often poorly conserved, even within a given viral family.
source: In contrast to viral genes such as Rep, with conserved enzymatic functions, sequences of the capsid genes are often poorly conserved, even within a given viral family (Buck et al., 2016).

claim: Capsid proteins have arisen repeatedly through capture and modification of different host cell proteins.

claim: iVireons is an artificial neural network trained by comparing alignment-independent variables between a large set of known viral structural proteins and known non-structural proteins.
source: We therefore turned to an alignment-independent approach known as iVireons, an artificial neural network trained by comparing alignment-independent variables between a large set of known viral structural proteins and known non-structural proteins (Seguritan et al., 2012) (https://vdm.sdsu.edu/ivireons/).

claim: Of the 17 DMGGs for which HHPRED did not identify capsid genes, iVireons predicted that ten contain at least one DMPC predicted to encode some type of virion structural protein.

claim: Several predicted capsid proteins formed roughly spherical particles when expressed in cell culture.
source: A subset of predicted capsid proteins were expressed in human-derived 293TT cells and/or in E. coli and subjected to size exclusion chromatography. Electron microscopic analysis showed that several of the predicted capsid proteins formed roughly spherical particles, whereas a negative control protein did not form particles (Figure 6).
evidence: This is shown in the electron microscopy images in Figure 6.

claim: A negative control protein did not form particles when expressed in cell culture.
source: A subset of predicted capsid proteins were expressed in human-derived 293TT cells and/or in E. coli and subjected to size exclusion chromatography. claim: The DMGC11 isolate ctgh70 preparation was found to contain nuclease-resistant nucleic acids, consistent with nonspecific encapsidation.
